September in the garden is a quiet turning point. The days are still full of life, but the light has changed, and the season is shifting. 

Here are some things to consider in the garden this month:

🌾 Harvest generously. Many plants respond to regular picking with one last burst of growth. Keep harvesting to encourage a final wave before the cooler days arrive.

🍅 Pick green tomatoes. If frost is on the horizon or your plants are slowing down, harvest unripe tomatoes and let them ripen indoors. 

🌿 Preserve your herbs. Gather herbs like basil, thyme, oregano, and mint for drying or freezing. A small harvest now means fresh flavor all winter long.

🌱 Plant cold-hardy crops. Kale, spinach, arugula, Swiss chard, corn salad, and leeks can still be planted in many regions. These crops are well adapted to cooler temperatures and shorter days.

💡 Start seeds indoors. Use a bright window, a small grow light setup, or a greenhouse to begin fall and winter crops. Even a little space can go a long way.

🌻 Leave some flowers standing. Let a few go to seed for next year’s harvest or to provide food for birds and overwintering insects.

🐝 Support pollinators. Bees and other beneficial insects are still active. Late-season blooms and a slightly untidy garden can make a real difference.

🌼 Plant for late color. Perennials like bluebeard offer one last splash of nectar-rich color when other flowers begin to fade.

🌸 Harvest flowers for drying or pressing. Now is the perfect time to preserve a bit of the season’s beauty.

📓 Take notes while it’s fresh. What’s thriving? What would you do differently next year? A few quick notes now can make spring planning much easier.

Subtle but SO important!

Part sun plants want 4–6 hours of sun, and prefer morning light, but can also handle afternoon sun. 

Part shade plants like morning sun, filtered light or a break from harsh afternoon rays.

If the plant tag says both, it’s flexible—but it still needs a few hours of direct rays on foliage sun.

If some of your plants get scorched leaves or foliage that fades, it means they need less direct sun. If they don’t flower as they should or become leggy, they need more.

How I attempt to fight back against the Squash Vine Borer.  In the past, I’ve been able to keep my pumpkins and squash going by injecting BT along the main stems/vines of the plants. 

When I have a lot of plants growing, this is tedious. But it’s a year where I have 4 zucchini plants, so not a huge deal. I get 1” needle/syringes, spray BT in a cup and go around injecting each stem about 4 times. 

Sometimes it’s tricky, the needles get clogged or you can’t get a good spot but as long as you get some in there, the vascular system of the plant should pull it up the vine and help you out. Grubs take some bites then bye bye! 👋 

I do this once a week once I start seeing eggs or the borer moth. Putting a link in my bio that has the stuff on Amazon - but you can find the syringes in pharmacies and BT in most garden centers.

Some of the best gardening advice I’ve ever received didn’t come from books or seed packets. It came from years of paying attention, making mistakes, and learning through experience.

Here are a few reminders from me @theknottygarden I come back to especially during the peak of the growing season when it’s easy to feel behind, overwhelmed, or unsure.

🌱 Your zone is a guideline, not a rule.
Hardiness zones are a starting point, not a limit. Microclimates, soil conditions, and growing techniques can all expand what’s possible.

📆 Gardens don’t follow calendars.
Seeds germinate when the conditions are right, not because the calendar says so. Tune in to your soil, weather, and plants, not just the date.

♻️ Don’t fear failure, compost it.
Every flop feeds your future. Mistakes teach us what works and what doesn’t and in the garden, even failure has value.

🌿 Say yes to the mess.
Not everything needs to be tidy. Leaves, stems, and wild corners are often the most alive and beneficial parts of your garden.

🪴 Garden soil is not the same as potting soil.
They serve different purposes. Potting soil is fluffy and well-draining for containers. Garden soil is dense, nutrient-rich, and teeming with life.

📦 Size matters when it come to containers.
Small pots dry out fast and limit root growth. The bigger the container, the more forgiving it is—especially in the heat of summer 

🍅 Don’t delay, harvest today.
Pick it when it’s ready. Waiting too long can mean overripening, pest damage, or plants slowing down. Frequent harvesting keeps things productive.

🌀 Gardens are never truly finished.
They evolve, just like we do. Don’t rush the process or stress about perfection. Growth takes time, and beauty lives in the in-between.

🌸 Take time to enjoy your garden.
Pause. Listen. Smell. Watch the bees. Pick a flower just because. A garden isn’t just a task list; it’s a living space meant to be loved. Thank you to my friend, Ket, for reminding me of this one.

🌿 Crowding plants might seem efficient, but it blocks crucial sunlight and airflow. Follow proper spacing guidelines - most vegetables need 12-18 inches between them.

Not all plants at the store are ready to thrive in your garden! In fact, I have seen them keep these boxes in the store for an entire year(none were alive). Before you bring home a box plant, 🪴 check for these three signs of health:

1️⃣ Look for New Growth 🌱 – Fresh, green shoots mean the plant is actively growing and thriving. If it looks dull and stagnant, it may be struggling.

2️⃣ Feel the Soil 🌍 – Gently open and squeeze the small bag of soil. If it’s still slightly moist, that’s a good sign! If it’s bone dry it might not make it.

3️⃣ Do the Scratch Test 🍃 – No visible new growth? Lightly scratch a small section of bark with your fingernail at the top. If it’s green underneath, the plant is still alive and has potential. If it’s brown and dry, move on!

Spring is here, and while your garden is bursting with life, it's also attracting some unwelcome visitors. Here's a comprehensive guide to common spring pests and how to keep them at bay:​

🐌 Snails & Slugs
These moisture-loving critters can decimate leaves and fruits overnight.​
Prevention: Avoid overwatering; spring rains often provide sufficient moisture.
Control: Handpick them during early morning or evening. Set up beer traps by burying shallow containers filled with beer at soil level to lure and drown them.

🐞 Aphids
Tiny sap-suckers that multiply rapidly, weakening plants.​
Prevention: Spray leaves with a mixture of water and dish soap to deter them.
Control: Wipe affected areas with rubbing alcohol or apply horticultural oil.

🕷️ Spider Mites
Microscopic pests that thrive in hot, dry conditions, causing stippled leaves.​
Prevention: Mist plants regularly to maintain humidity.
Control: Use horticultural oil sprays and wipe leaves with rubbing alcohol.

🦟 Whiteflies
Small white insects that feed on plant juices, leaving sticky residue.​
Prevention: Apply a water and dish soap solution to leaves.
Control: Alternate between soapy water and neem oil sprays.

🐛 Caterpillars & Worms
Leaf-munching larvae that can cause significant damage.​
Prevention: Plant strong-scented herbs to deter them.
Control: Handpick or apply Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) spray.
​
🌿 Gardener's Tip: Maintain healthy soil and plant diversity to naturally deter pests. Regularly inspect your plants and act promptly at the first sign of trouble.

Are you afraid of growing mint with other plants because you’ve heard it’s too invasive and won’t allow other crops to grow? 

I used to be afraid of growing mint with others too, until I found a way to make it work.👇

🌿1. Always grow mint in a contained space such as a pot or raised bed. Avoid growing it directly in the ground.

🌿2.  Mint is excellent for pest control in the garden as its smell repels many pests like aphids, flea beetles, squash bugs, cabbage moth butterflies, whiteflies and more. Use it as a companion plant to grow next to tomatoes, peppers and eggplants, brassicas like cabbage, broccoli, kale and cauliflower and of course herbs like basil and dill (as they have similar watering requirements).

🌿3. To prevent mint from taking over completely, be sure to harvest often. 

🌿4. Drape mint runners over the sides of the container or raised bed to give other plants sufficient space to grow.

I love my little mint, basil and dill planter so much and would definitely do it again next year. Hope you try it too! ✨

What is a Potager garden? 

A French-inspired kitchen garden where edible plants like vegetables, fruits, and herbs are artfully arranged with flowers to create a visually beautiful, functional, and productive space. 
Historically used to supply fresh produce for the kitchen, potagers can range from formal, symmetrical designs with structured beds and pathways to more informal, romantic styles reminiscent of English cottage gardens. Chard! 🌱 

This sunset chard has been lighting up the allotment since last year and is growing so much with the warm weather we’ve been having! 

Chard, which is also known as Swiss chard, is a leafy green vegetable with a mild, slightly sweet taste, similar to spinach but with a stronger flavor. It’s a member of the beet family and has large, crinkled leaves attached to thick, crunchy stems. 

You can eat chard raw in salads, cooked like spinach, or used in various dishes. I like to use mine in pasta dishes, stews and casseroles and in wraps as a green leaf. 

I start my chard seeds off in the greenhouse in early spring and I multi sow them which means I sow more than one seed in each module. When they are around 5cm tall I garden them off and plant them out. I’ll then do another sowing, directly into the growing site, around July/August to overwinter giving me crops through winter and into early spring and the hungry gap.

As an organic gardener, I don’t use old tires for raised bed gardening. Although it may be a good way to repurpose waste, tires are made with some not so friendly ingredients. Here’s a list of things that can be found in a tire:
Acetone
Aniline
Arsenic
Barium
Benzene (a known carcinogen)
Benzothiazole
Cadmium
Chloroethane
Chromium
Cobalt
Copper
Halogenated flame retardants
Isoprene
Latex
Lead
Manganese
Mercury
Methyl ethyl ketone
Methyl isobutyl ketone
Naphthalene
Nickel
Nylon
Phenol
Pigments
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH), suspected as a carcinogen
Polyester
Rayon
Styrene‑butadiene (suspected as a carcinogen)
Toluene
Trichloroethylene

Even though it may take years for some of these things to make it into the soil, even though it may just be trace amounts, it’s enough to pollute the soil and your body. Especially over a longer period of time or for the renters/owners after you leave. If you think about the mapping of DNA, all it takes is one small mutation of one gene to cause defects. It can be a butterfly effect. Now some might say ‘Ok I’ll just do decorative/non edible plants in the tires’ but you have to remember we aren’t the only ones eating the plants. Harmful chemicals also effect the bees and other pollinators/animals that feed on plants not consumed by humans. My own belief is that it’s best to keep absolutely everything as organic and as close to how nature would do it as possible. Be mindful of what you are planting in. It can also be dangerous to plant in containers (like certain plastic storage tubs) that weren’t made to be food safe.

The five principles of organic gardening 

#4 increase biodiversity

Simply put, ‘biodiversity’ means many different life forms. For the gardener, this can be done in three simple ways:

Growing different types of plants, so that a variety of flowers, vegetables, trees and shrubs are all present.

Providing habitats and food for wildlife such as birds, insects and mammals. They are not only a delight to look at, but each species has its role in maintaining a natural balance.

And feeding the soil life. Healthy soil is full of bacteria, fungi, microbes and creatures which create the right environment for plants to thrive, releasing nutrients and creating good soil structure.

With this variety of different species, all working together, the organic grower encourages a healthy interdependency between plants and wildlife.

A full border of mixed flowers and shrubs will not only give yourself year round interest but will encourage a range of wildlife too. Even a species rich lawn(full of weeds😉) plays its part.

SUCCESSION PLANTING - The Key to Season Round Harvests this Summer

A key lesson I learnt in my third or fourth year of growing my veggies - get seeds started early and KEEP ON PLANTING - all spring long.

In our harsh climate here in Australia, giving seedlings an early start is critical for them to survive our summers. But it’s also critical to give yourself time to succession plant.

Succession planting is when you stagger the sowing of your seeds so that your crops mature at different times and you have a set of back up seedlings ready and available to plant in the event of pests or disease in your main garden.

Sunday's first-ever open garden event was SO FREAKING GOOD – joyful, connective, fun and waaaay more work than we expected. 😅

Still kinda riding the high.

Here are a few photos from the sold-out half-day experience at my little urban permaculture demonstration site just outside Tarntanya / Adelaide’s city centre.

We started with a practical session on small-space permaculture garden design, then explored lesser-known edible plants that thrive in South Australia’s dry, often-hot conditions.

And we wrapped up with a shared sit-down lunch pumping with garden produce. The nasturtium leaf dolmades and fresh-picked peas with homemade labneh were crowd faves.

It was so cool watching new connections form among like-minded locals – a big reason we structured the day with plenty of time for interaction. Our little way of growing the mycelial network of strong, supportive community.

Everything went off without a hitch, despite a thunderstorm and hectic downpour that somehow cleared to blue skies just before we started 😳 … and the oven dying juuuust as Kym began cooking lunch 😬

Huge thanks to the legends who came along and shared this beautiful day (and Kym’s MANY puns) with us.

And yep, we're already dreaming up ways to open the garden again.

My long-held vision is to offer this space as a living example of what’s possible on a small city block — how you can use permaculture to grow food, increase biodiversity, cool your home and create beauty. And how all that's doable even if you’re short on time or energy, or live with mobility or health limitations (like me).

So, if you’d like to hear about future events, hop on my newsletter list (link in bio) — my email crew are always first to know about new happenings. 👌

The five principles of organic gardening 

#5 Maintain a healthy growing area

A diverse and vigorous growing system, good hygiene, and close observation all help prevent problems.

Keeping your growing area in good health, rather than just pest and disease free, is at the heart of organic growing. Creating a diverse and vigorous growing system, good hygiene, and close observation all help prevent problems.

To achieve a healthy growing area, you should:

Keep your soil in good condition.

Source healthy plants which are well suited to where they will grow.

Be observant – often problems arise from failing to spot the first signs of disease. Frequent and early intervention prevents problems from escalating.

Practise good hygiene.

Reposted from @urbangardeningschool As an organic gardener, I don’t use old tires for raised bed gardening. Although it may be a good way to repurpose waste, tires are made with some not so friendly ingredients. Here’s a list of things that can be found in a tire:
Acetone
Aniline
Arsenic
Barium
Benzene (a known carcinogen)
Benzothiazole
Cadmium
Chloroethane
Chromium
Cobalt
Copper
Halogenated flame retardants
Isoprene
Latex
Lead
Manganese
Mercury
Methyl ethyl ketone
Methyl isobutyl ketone
Naphthalene
Nickel
Nylon
Phenol
Pigments
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH), suspected as a carcinogen
Polyester
Rayon
Styrene‑butadiene (suspected as a carcinogen)
Toluene
Trichloroethylene

Even though it may take years for some of these things to make it into the soil, even though it may just be trace amounts, it’s enough to pollute the soil and your body. Especially over a longer period of time or for the renters/owners after you leave. If you think about the mapping of DNA, all it takes is one small mutation of one gene to cause defects. It can be a butterfly effect. Now some might say ‘Ok I’ll just do decorative/non edible plants in the tires’ but you have to remember we aren’t the only ones eating the plants. Harmful chemicals also effect the bees and other pollinators/animals that feed on plants not consumed by humans. My own belief is that it’s best to keep absolutely everything as organic and as close to how nature would do it as possible. Be mindful of what you are planting in. It can also be dangerous to plant in containers (like certain plastic storage tubs) that weren’t made to be food safe.

Here a collection of the pests I have found in my garden so far. A note from an organic gardener:
- Orange Assassin Bug (not a pest) I’ve experienced orange footed nymphs some years ago and though that’s what this was, so I took a photo. It was eating an ant. A known pest in my garden. So I let it be, went inside looked it up and found this bug isn’t native to my area and isn’t a pest. 
-I’ve been seeing some damage to my upper tomato leaves but yet to find the culprit. 
- I found some white flies here and there but after the infestation our town had a few years ago, this isn’t bad and I’m not seeing any damage they’ve done yet. 
-the tomato leaf looks odd and this could be a number of things but for now this leaf is the only one like this. 
- evidence of leaf miners has sown up on my cucumbers and squash plants. I find this typical. Its more devastating to smaller plants like beans which so far have none. 
- I have about 5 different species of ants in my garden this year, the most problematic are the black ants on the lemon tree and red ants on my bean plant. I spray them with cold water, but I’m about ready to ramp up to organic pesticides. 
- not the ladybug, the brown marmorated beetle photobombing. It’s a member of the stink bug family and they are bad for citrus and low and behold it’s on my mandarin tree. 
- little harder to see but same family, green soldier bug also know for being a bother to citrus plants. 
- harlequin bugs I found him on my nasturtium plant which I plants for the bugs. They usually like members of the brassica family, none of which are currently in my garden for this reason I would be treating. Though I usually had pick these guys. 
- roly poly not normally a pest as they amend soil through break down organic material. But I have thousands in my garden. They can be seen in broad daylight just walking around because their population has gotten out of hand. Do they eat my healthy plants now.

Blank Space… not such a good thing in the vegetable garden, for several reasons. Nature doesn’t like blank spaces. Look around if you’re out for a hike, you rarely see bare dirt, something always fills it in. In your vegetable garden this is usually in the form of weeds. Blank spaces in the garden also tend to dry out faster, even if they’re mulched they don’t hold moisture as well as when they’re shaded by growth. Perhaps the most important reason why blank space is no good in a vegetable garden is that space that could be providing food! 

So why am I showing you blank spaces in my garden? There’s a lot of reasons we end up with spots like this. In the first two pictures the things I planted there just didn’t make it. The second two pictures are the beds where I previously had garlic growing. The good news is you can always fill blank spaces! I will be planting quick growing fall crops in these spaces this week. Things like lettuce, carrots, radishes, and beets that love the cooler weather of fall. 

Check back later to see how these blank spaces got filled in!

A few weeks ago, I put a poll on my stories to get to know this small but mighty community on Instagram. The results were split 50/50 with just half of us gardening organically. 
The main reason was ‘not knowing enough’ which I can understand as it used to be me! 
.
What does it mean to be an organic gardener? 
🌱- Simply put, gardening naturally and without the use of chemicals. As gardeners, we have the opportunity to choose what we put on our plants. It’s completely up to us what effect we have in our garden. 
.
Where do I start? 
🌱 - Start with your compost and ditch the peat! There are lots of fantastic peat and chemical free composts available. 
🌱 - Control pests naturally! We’ve all rushed to the garden centre and picked the first slug defence we can find, desperately trying to protect our precious seedlings. Most pesticides unfortunately contain chemicals that have devastating effects on our environment and wildlife 💔🦔 
.

It's time to prepare your lawn for Spring!

💧 Be ready to turn your sprinklers back on on the 1st of September.

🌧  WA has had plenty of rain over winter, so the ground is still holding moisture. But as the weather warms up, your lawn can quickly become stressed without water. Don’t let it dry out completely. Start thinking ahead now.
 See info below, or use the link for the detailed pdf ➡️ 
https://greenacresturfgroup.com.au/how-to-get-your-lawn-ready-for-spring/

3 STEPS
1️⃣ CUPS 
Catch Cups are ideal and available complimentary here at Greenacres Turf Group; however any straight-sided container is suitable (Ice cream containers, coffee cups) marking 10mm up the sides. Start your irrigation system and assess that all the sprinklers are working and there are no obstructions eg. the grass has not grown higher than the sprinklers.

2️⃣ CALIBRATION 
Place the Catch Cups randomly over the lawn, turn your sprinklers on for 10 minutes & then measure the contents to determine that your sprinklers are spraying evenly. Check sprinkler nozzles & filter and flush to remove any debris.

3️⃣ FERTILISE
Our WA soils are often high in silica and low in water retention. To help lock in moisture, apply a Soil Wetter and Moisture Retainer:
💧Start with Aqua Force (follow label directions)
💧Then apply Bi-Agra 5 days later

Repeat every 4–6 weeks through the warmer months

🌱As the soil warms up, your lawn is waking up from winter dormancy and will benefit from a good feed. Use a balanced, slow-release NPK fertiliser to kick-start strong, healthy growth

Today’s story is all about my recent terrace garden harvest! 🌿🌞
As we come to the end of summer, some of these veggies mark the final harvest of the season—while a few like amaranthus just don’t seem to leave my garden! They pop up here and there, and I let a few grow fully while leaving others for seeds. You’ll spot them in today’s harvest.

Sorrel varieties are also in the basket—you just need to keep plucking and pinching them. They reward you by branching out and being ready for the next harvest in just a week!
A special mention goes to ponaganti kura—a complete invader in my garden. It claims every container by simply touching the soil and rooting at every node. While it’s nutritious, removing it is such a task—it’s rooted deep and keeps popping back up no matter what!

I’ve also harvested a few volunteer ash gourds. These sprouted from seeds I added while layering compost two months ago. They grew over the compost and flourished just in time before the rainy season kicked in—my bonus crops!

And oh, the dragon fruits—they only need water and no other care. Yet, they reward me year after year! 🍉🌵

This time, I’ve also added a new variety—elephant tusk okra (Tusk okra)—and have transplanted them along with cucumbers. The cucumbers are now cleared, and these okras have taken over those containers.

So, today’s harvest is a perfect example of how you can continue growing food without any break between seasons. If you’d like to understand the process in detail, I’ve pinned the video in the comments & story.🌱

🌿 Spinach + Radishes → Radishes mature early, leaving room for spinach.

Some garden truths aren’t found in seed packets or how-to videos.

They’re learned by doing—by paying attention. Here are the lessons that stick with you long after harvest.

💧 Moving water is magic.
It invites life—frogs, birds, dragonflies—and oxygenates your space. A small fountain or stream makes your garden pulse with energy.

🌿 Vertical growing is essential.
Limited on space? Go up. Vining crops love it, airflow improves, and harvests become easier. Every layer of space can grow something.

🔁 Succession plant everything.
When one plant’s done, another goes in. This rhythm keeps beds productive and pollinators busy. Food and flowers alike—don’t let soil sit bare.

🌈 Variety brings resilience.
Monocultures are fragile. Mix colors, bloom times, species. Heirlooms + hybrids, annuals + perennials—intentional variety builds a bulletproof ecosystem.

🌱 Soil is everything.
Forget quick fixes. Compost, mulch, microbes—this is where life begins. Feed the soil, and the soil will feed the garden.

👣 The gardener’s shadow is the best fertilizer.
Presence matters. Walk, observe, touch, listen. The more you see, the better you respond. Your care is what cultivates abundance.

🌸 No flowers = no food.
Veggies depend on pollinators. Pollinators depend on blooms. Interplant flowers not just for beauty, but for the bees. It’s all connected.

🦋 Diversity = biodiversity.
Each plant invites different life. Together, they form a balanced, resilient web. More species = fewer problems and more joy.

🪺 A garden is an ecosystem.
It’s not just plants—it’s bugs, birds, bacteria, weather. Build relationships between living things, and watch your garden stabilize.

🎨 Plants don’t care about pretty.
They care about what helps them grow: soil, light, water. Ditch perfection. Embrace wild, messy, working beauty.

🐛 If nothing’s eating your garden… that’s a problem.
A garden with no pests is a garden with no predators. A few holes mean your ecosystem is alive and working as it should.

From my garden to yours,

🌸Erin

Chard! 🌱 

This sunset chard has been lighting up the allotment since last year and is growing so much with the warm weather we’ve been having! 

Chard, which is also known as Swiss chard, is a leafy green vegetable with a mild, slightly sweet taste, similar to spinach but with a stronger flavor. It’s a member of the beet family and has large, crinkled leaves attached to thick, crunchy stems. 

You can eat chard raw in salads, cooked like spinach, or used in various dishes. I like to use mine in pasta dishes, stews and casseroles and in wraps as a green leaf. 

I start my chard seeds off in the greenhouse in early spring and I multi sow them which means I sow more than one seed in each module. When they are around 5cm tall I garden them off and plant them out. I’ll then do another sowing, directly into the growing site, around July/August to overwinter giving me crops through winter and into early spring and the hungry gap.

🌱 Healthy soil = healthy plants. Here’s my simple organic fertilizing rhythm that keeps the garden thriving season after season:

– Compost or soil conditioner each season
– Fish emulsion right after planting
– A balanced organic fertilizer as plants grow
– Tomato-Tone or Big Bloom during fruiting
– Bt spray, milk + water, and daily checks for pests & disease

It doesn’t have to be complicated — just consistent. Healthy soil, organic products, and steady care = abundant harvests 🤍

Check for Poops, Then Get Ready to Pick!

Those little green nuggets? Yep… hornworm poop. 🐛 And if you see it, you’ve got a tomato thief hiding out, blending in like a pro.

Step 1️⃣ Pick off every hornworm you can find.
Step 2️⃣ Clear away the poops.
Step 3️⃣ Come back tomorrow… if there’s new poop, the sneaky bandit is STILL there!

Start the hunt all over again. Did you know? A single hornworm can eat an entire tomato plant in just one night!

If you just can’t find them all, grab a Bt spray—it’s safe for organic gardening but spray it in the evening to protect your pollinators. Anyone who thinks gardening is peaceful clearly hasn’t been in a midnight showdown with these green eating machines…

Let’s get specific, What to plant in July & August (local subtropical region)

I get asked this all the time 
 “What can I grow here?”
“Why are my plants dying?”

The truth is, what works in one part of the country might fail miserably somewhere else.
We’re subtropical here, and as always timing matters, especially in winter!

Right now (July & August) we’re at the tail end of our cool season seed planting, (mine were planted Feb/ March ) but there’s still plenty you can sow from seed to make the most of it….

🥬 Veggies
– Lettuce
– Kale
– Silverbeet
– Carrots
– Beetroot
– Snow peas
- Onions
– Radish
– Spring onions
– Broccoli & cabbage (pretty much July only, so now’s the time!)

🌿 Herbs
– Coriander
– Parsley
– Dill
– Chives
– Thyme
– Oregano

🌸 Flowers
– Calendula
– Violas
– Nasturtiums
– Alyssum
– Sweet peas (if you’re quick!)
- Sunflowers (grow nearly all year here for me)

Planting in the right season sets you up for success, healthy plants, fewer pests, and actual harvests. 🌿
Just because it’s for sale in a seed packet doesn’t mean it will grow well right now where you are, if at all! Take Rhubarb… it might grow for a while but I’ve never had much success in subtropical conditions! It likes the cold! 

Stick with what suits our local climate now and you’ll be harvesting before spring even begins….
